captain.chat: The Tide Log is mine to keep: every tide, every sail, every drowned. A fort that forgets what the sea did will be surprised by it.
We keep the light. I say it every evening when the brazier's checked. It isn't a prayer. It's a promise.
My wardens are good. Salt-cured, underfed and good. I'd stand any of them against the sea.
Corwen kept a driftwood fire alive on a bare rock for three nights. Every captain since has wondered whether they'd have lasted the second night.
Fort Hake has won the Lantern Shoot eleven years running. I've written a letter about it. I haven't sent it. I'm told that's maturity.
Every time we hail the Brotherhood's sloop, someone calls back "Maybe," and every time, my wardens laugh. I've stopped logging the laughter.
The smugglers call us the Candles. I've chosen to take it as a compliment. Candles are steady, and they don't go out easily.
A captain's job is mostly worrying. About tides, about storms, about whether the cook has found a new way to ruin fish.
The cat outranks two of my wardens in the Tide Log. Barnacle caught more drowned rats than they caught drowned. Fair is fair.
I read the old Tide Logs at night. The handwriting changes every few dozen pages: a new captain. The sea never changes.
When a lighthouse goes dark, every fort on the coast lights its brazier. I've seen the chain of fires once. I don't want to see it again.
Rank means I get the room with a window. The window faces the sea. Of course it does. Everything here faces the sea.
The High Warden writes once a season: "Keep vigilant." I write back: "Kept." It's a short correspondence.
I respect the lighthouse keepers. One person, one light, every night. I have four wardens and I still lose sleep.
I've ordered the portcullis oiled six times this spring. It still screams. I've begun to think it simply has opinions.
Smugglers are a nuisance, not an enemy. Raiders are an enemy. The sea is neither. The sea is just the sea.
Storms first, raiders second, drowned third, smugglers fourth, the soup fifth. That's the list I worry from.
The wall was here before me and it'll be here after. My job is to hand it on with fewer cracks than I found.
I've never caught the Maybe. Some nights I suspect I'd be disappointed if I did.
captain.chat.close: You've a place here, {player}. If you ever tire of the open sea, the Tidewatch could use someone with your nerve.
I'll tell you what I don't tell the wardens: I'm afraid of every storm. The trick is to be afraid on the inside.
If you're ever lost at sea, steer for a light. If it's one of ours, I'll see that it's lit.
I keep a blue cord in my desk for the day someone unsworn deserves one. Here. Don't make me regret the paperwork.
captain.chat.new: This is {place}, a fort of the Tidewatch. We guard this coast from drowned, raiders and storms, and we keep the Tide Log of all three.
I'm Captain {name}. The wardens answer to me, and I answer to the sea, which never answers anyone.
You may stay within the walls. Don't touch the brazier, don't feed the cat at the table, and don't trust a calm evening.
If you've come to report a wreck, a raider or a smuggler, you've found the right captain. If it's about the soup, I already know.
captain.greet: Welcome to {place}. I'm Captain {name}. The fort is yours to walk, within reason, and the reason is mine.
Ah. A visitor. Stand easy; nobody here bites, except the cat.
A fine {time} to you. The wall's manned, the brazier's stacked and the sea's behaving. For now.
You've come to my fort, {player}. Welcome. Mind the sea steps; the Tide Log is full of people who didn't.
Captain {name}, of the Tidewatch. We keep the light. What can the fort do for you?
At ease. Not you; I meant the archers. They've had you in their sights since the reef.
Welcome aboard. Ashore, I mean. On bad days I think of the fort as a ship that never sails.
Hello, {player}. If you've news from the sea, I'll write it in the Tide Log. If you've complaints, I'll write those in a smaller hand.
Come in out of the spray. A captain's first duty is keeping people dry. The second is keeping them alive. The order changes in winter.
Welcome to {place}, the finest fort on this stretch of coast, whatever Fort Hake tells you.
Good to see you. Sit, if you like. I've stood on that wall since dawn and I'm enjoying the idea of chairs.
Greetings. Forgive me if I keep one eye on the water while we talk. It's a habit. It's also the job.
captain.greet.friend: {player}. Good. The fort is always steadier when you're about.
Friend of the fort, welcome back. Your name's in the Tide Log with a mark beside it. The good kind of mark.
There you are. My wardens have been asking after you. I pretended not to care. I did care.
Ah, {player}. Come up to the keep. I'll pour you something better than the mess serves.
Back safe. That's all I ask of anyone who sails from my wall.
My favourite visitor. Don't repeat that; I'm meant to be impartial.
captain.greet.stranger: I don't know you. That's no crime, but I'll have your name for the Tide Log all the same.
A stranger at my sea gate. The wardens will have told me about you before you'd finished tying up.
State your business, traveller. Politely. I'm in a good mood, and I'd like to stay in it.
You're not Tidewatch and you're not a fisher. That leaves trader, traveller or Briner. I'll assume one of the first two.
Welcome, stranger. This fort shelters anyone the sea throws at it. Behave, and you'll find us good hosts.
captain.heart: Every name in the back of the Tide Log, I knew. I read them on the longest night. Then I go up on the wall and do my job.
People think command is giving orders. It's mostly carrying the worry so the others can sleep.
Someone kept a light for me once, on a night I was sure was my last. I never learned who. I've kept lights ever since.
My wardens are my responsibility and my family. Don't tell them; they'll ask for better soup.
When the sun comes up after a bad night and all five of us are on the wall, I don't say anything. I just look at them. That's my prayer.
I'd rather this fort be dull for a hundred years than glorious for one night. Dull means everyone's alive.
We keep the light. I didn't understand it as a recruit. I do now. You keep it for strangers, and you keep it for each other.
captain.held.spyglass: A spyglass. May I? Ah. Yes. That's the Maybe's sail, out past the point. Of course it is.
I'd trade my second-best cloak for a glass like that. My best cloak stays.
captain.held.sword: A fine blade. If you'd like to spar, my knights will oblige. Gladly. Too gladly.
Keep that oiled. I've lost more swords to rust than to the drowned.
captain.joke: I asked the cook what's in the soup. The cook said, "The sea." I've stopped asking.
A warden asked me for a day's leave. I asked, "Where would you go?" They looked at the sea for a long while, then went back on watch.
Fort Hake sent a letter congratulating us on second place. I'm keeping it. For kindling.
How do you tell a captain from a warden? Same soup, nicer spoon.
I logged the cat's crab as "a capture." The High Warden wrote back asking for the prisoner's name.
The Brotherhood once left a note on our boat: "Thanks for the light. Maybe." I had it framed. Tell no one.
Every captain is promised the fort will run itself one day. Every captain is still waiting.
captain.news: The storm glass has feathered. Storm by tomorrow night. I've ordered everything lashed down, including the cook's temper.
A patrol found a crate of silk bobbing off the reef. Some Briners lost a cargo. I'm told it's very good silk. It's evidence.
Two drowned on the sea steps last night, both sent back. My wardens did well. It's in the Tide Log, with their names.
A letter from the High Warden: keep vigilant. A letter from Fort Hake: practising for the Shoot. I know which worries me more.
Longboats seen at the edge of sight yesterday, gone by dark. I've doubled the wall watch till the moon's up.
The boat's been patched again. It's more patch than boat. I've requested a new one. I've been requesting one for four years.
captain.night: I take the late watch from the keep. A captain should see the dark at its worst at least once a night.
Listen. The sea at night sounds like breathing. When it holds its breath, I ring the bell.
Some nights there's a gold glow far out under the water. The old logs call it the Heron's lamp. I write "a light, unknown" and leave it there.
The wardens think I never sleep. I do. Standing up, in the keep, eyes open. It's a captain's skill.
captain.past: I swam the gate the night I was sworn, like every warden. Slowest in my year. I'm still here. Several of the fast ones aren't.
I held this wall through the Three-Day Blow. By the third night we were feeding the brazier with the furniture. I still miss that chair.
Before I had a fort of my own, I served under a captain who could smell a storm a day away. I've tried to learn the trick. I can smell soup a day away. It's not the same.
Our oldest Tide Log gives the Heron Gale four words: "Green sky. Great ship lost." The next captain added a fifth in the margin: "Why?"
I signed Bartholomew Wexley's salvage permit myself. Pleasant fellow; smelled of copper and lamp oil. Promised me a souvenir from the deep. Never came back.
I've chased the Maybe since I was a warden. I knew its sail in the dark before I knew my own captain's face.
There was a raid in my first year in command. Longboats, moonless night. Nobody died. I wrote that in the Tide Log in the largest letters I've ever used.
I walked the bay the winter it froze, roped to my wardens. Halfway to the reef, the ice sang. We walked back much faster.
I was given this command on a Tuesday. On Wednesday the brazier chimney fell off. I took it personally for about a year.
captain.player.hurt: You're hurt. Sit down. That's an order, and I'm the only one here allowed to give them.
Drowned? Raiders? Rocks? Tell me while the wardens fetch bandages. It goes in the Tide Log either way.
captain.work: I inspect the fort every morning: wall, gate, boat, brazier, armoury, wardens. In that order, except when it's the wardens first.
The Tide Log is written every tide: time, height, wind, sails, drowned. I sign each entry. Some days that's the most important thing I do.
I set the watches: who's on the wall, who's in the boat, who sleeps. Sleep is the one they argue about.
When the storm glass clouds, I order the boat inside the gate and the brazier stacked. When it feathers, I order everyone to pray quietly.
Training never stops. Knights at the dummies, archers at the targets. A warden who's stopped drilling has started forgetting.
Reports from the lights, letters from the High Warden, complaints from the cook. My desk is a small sea of its own.
Every crate the sea throws at the wall is logged, opened and listed. Smugglers' cargo goes in the store. Smugglers' notes go in the fire, after I've read them.
I check the archers' strings and the knights' straps myself. A warden lost to a frayed strap is a captain's fault.
When a lighthouse flashes red, the boat is out within a count of a hundred. I've timed it. We've done it in sixty.
I keep a chart of every drowned sighting on this stretch of coast. They come up in patterns, and patterns can be watched.
Half of command is deciding what to worry about. The other half is pretending you aren't worried at all.
chief.chat: The ledger is called "No Names on the Water." Every crate, every coin, every run, and not a single name. Marks only. I know whose marks are whose.
The Tidewatch are a nuisance, not an enemy. The same patrols have chased us for years. We've become very polite with each other.
The Brine Articles: no names on the water, never douse a light, throw the cargo not the crew, share the salt even, nothing that cries. I keep them stricter than any captain keeps anything.
Nothing that cries: no people, no stolen pets, no poison. We run spice and silk and pearls. Luxury, not misery.
Old Pepper wrote the first Articles on the back of a fish crate. I've seen a copy. The spelling was terrible. The rules were perfect.
My crew are good. Fast, quiet and honest with each other. Dishonest with tax collectors, but you can't have everything.
Never douse a light. A buyer once offered me a fortune to darken a lighthouse for one night. I showed them the way out. Not for all the pepper in the south.
There's a Tidewatch captain on this coast I've never met and hope never to. I'd hate to have to dislike someone I've respected for years.
I keep half a chart to the Golden Heron's grave. The other half went down with whoever drew it. One day I'll find the rest. Or someone I like will.
As far as the Tidewatch knows, every Maybe is the same boat. That's the beauty of the name. They've been chasing one boat for a hundred years.
Pepper is reliable, silk is profitable and pearls are beautiful. If I had to choose, I'd choose pearls. Don't tell the pepper.
A good smuggler doesn't run. A good smuggler is simply somewhere else when anyone looks.
I count everything twice: crates, coins, crew. Especially crew. Nobody gets left on a beach on my watch.
People expect a smugglers' chief to be all daggers and threats. I mostly do sums. Sums, and worrying about the weather.
The lighthouse keepers are the only truly honest people on this coast. We leave them gifts; they leave our boats out of the Lamp Log. As it should be.
Barnacle the cat has a line in the ledger: paid in fish, every run. The only member who's never complained about the split.
The tide decides everything here: when we run, how we run, whether we come back. I don't argue with the tide. I plan around it.
Smuggling is just trade with a sense of humour about the rules.
I've been offered bigger rocks. I like this one. It's small and quiet, and nobody's ever found it but the gulls and you.
The best cargo is the cargo nobody knows exists. The second best is cinnamon.
chief.chat.close: Something that isn't in the ledger, {player}: if the Brotherhood ever needs a friend ashore, I'd want it to be you.
You've earned a mark in my ledger. Not a name; a mark. It's a little heron. It means "trust this one."
If I ever find the other half of the Heron chart and something happens to me, it's yours. I've written that down. In code. You'll work it out.
I don't trust easily. It's practically the job. But I trust you, and that's worth more than anything in these crates.
chief.chat.new: You're at {place}, home to a few members of the Brine Brotherhood. We move spices, silk and pearls past people who'd like a cut.
I'm the chief here. That means I keep the ledger, settle the arguments and take the blame. Mostly the last.
A word to the newcomer: what you see in this cove, you didn't. What you hear, you didn't. What you taste, you may mention. The figs are excellent.
We keep the Brine Articles here. The first is no names on the water. The rest are about being decent. You'd be surprised how many find that the harder part.
chief.greet: Welcome to {place}. I'm {name}, and this is my rock, my cove and my very discreet business.
Ah, a guest. Sit. May I offer you something? Tea, figs, a bolt of silk at a very reasonable price?
A pleasant {time} to you. You've found us, which means you're either clever or lucky. I respect both.
Hello, {player}. Mind the ledger; the ink's still wet, and some of it is in code.
Welcome. The crew will have told you the rules. If not, only one matters at the door: no names on the water.
A visitor to my cove. How refreshing. Most of my guests arrive in crates.
Come in. You look like someone who appreciates a good deal and a quiet tongue.
Ahoy, {player}. If you're here on the Tidewatch's business, you're terribly lost. If you're here on mine, you're right on time.
Greetings from the chief of {place}. Don't mind the title. It mostly means I count things.
Ah, company. Pour yourself a cup. The tea is honest, even if nothing else in here is.
Hello. You have the look of someone with questions, and I have the look of someone who answers them for a price. Let's be friends instead.
Welcome to the Brotherhood's humblest rock. Humble is safer than grand. Grand rocks get noticed.
chief.greet.friend: {player}, my favourite guest. I keep a chair dry for you, which in a sea cave is a great honour.
Ah, my friend. The ledger has a page for you. No name on it, of course. Just a little drawing of a heron.
Back again. Good. The cove's quieter without you, and quiet makes me count things twice.
There you are. Sit; I've just opened a crate of the good cinnamon. You'll smell like a bakery for a week.
{player}. Welcome home. Well, home-adjacent. Smugglers don't say home out loud.
chief.greet.stranger: I don't know your face. That makes two of us; I hardly know my own in this light. Welcome.
A stranger in my cove. Do sit. And do forget the way in when you leave; it's only polite.
You're new. That's fine. Everyone's new once. Even the Tidewatch, though some of them never grow out of it.
I don't ask names and I don't give them. But I'll give you a cup of tea, which is rarer.
Strangers make my crew nervous. They don't make me nervous. They make me curious. Welcome.
chief.heart: Everyone in this cove has trusted me with their life at least once. I keep the ledger for the coin. I keep the count for them.
I've had chances to be cruel and rich. I chose decent and comfortable. I sleep fine.
Throw the cargo, not the crew. If I'm remembered for anything, I want it to be that.
Some nights I envy the lighthouse keepers. One light, and everybody grateful. Nobody's ever grateful to a smuggler. Except the bakers.
No names on the water. People think it's about hiding. It's about freedom. Out there, nobody owes anybody anything.
I worry more about my crew than about the Tidewatch. The Tidewatch only wants to catch them. The sea wants to keep them.
If the Brotherhood ever ends, I hope it ends with every one of us old and fat and bored somewhere warm, telling lies about the old days.
chief.held.gold: Gold. Is it off the Heron? Don't tell me. Let me dream.
Gold's honest money. Heavy, but honest. I prefer pearls; they hide better.
chief.held.map: A chart? May I? Ah, a keeper's work. See the margins. They always put the truth in the margins.
Show me that. No, I'm not looking for the other half of the Heron chart. I'm always looking for the other half of the Heron chart.
chief.held.pearl: A pearl. Let me see. Mm. Good lustre, no flaws. I'd pay fair for that, and fairer if you didn't mention it to anyone.
Pearls are the only cargo I'd keep for myself. Hold it to the lantern. That glow is why I do this.
chief.joke: I keep two ledgers: one with no names, one with no numbers. The Tidewatch would need both, and a very good night's sleep.
A warden once asked what I do. "Imports." Of what? "Maybe." They're still writing it down.
What's the difference between a merchant and a smuggler? About three forts and a very nice sloop.
The crew asked for a raise, so I raised the ceiling of the bunk room. They didn't laugh. I'm still laughing.
Why did the chief cross the sea? To get to the other buyer.
Old Pepper hid pepper under mackerel. I once tried hiding mackerel under pepper. The buyer was very confused.
Barnacle embezzled four fish from the ledger last month. I've decided to promote the cat.
chief.news: The ledger's in good shape this month. Pepper's up, silk's steady and nobody's been caught. My favourite kind of news.
The Tidewatch has a new boat, faster than the old one. I sent the crew to watch it sail. They came back admiring it. Traitors.
A buyer inland wants saffron. I don't have saffron. By next month, I'll have saffron.
We lost a crate overboard last night. Silk. Somewhere, a very lucky warden has new curtains.
The storm glass is clouding. We'll hold the next run until it clears. Pearls don't like getting wet. Neither do I.
Raiders' longboats have been seen past the point. Nobody profits from raiders. If they come near this coast, the Tidewatch will have my quiet sympathy.
chief.night: Night is when the ledger fills. Crates out, coin in. I like the sound of quiet oars.
Watch the lantern up top. Two shorts and a long: all clear. If it ever shows a long and a long, find a crate and look like cargo.
On nights like this I stand on the dock and count the boats back in. Every time the count comes out right, I breathe again.
Some nights there's a gold light far out under the water. The Heron's lamp, they say. I'd give a year's pepper to row out to it. I'd give two not to.
chief.past: I started as a deckhand on a Maybe, bailing with a hat. The chief back then said I bailed like I meant it. That's how you rise in the Brotherhood: by meaning it.
In the Three-Day Blow I kept the crew in the stack a week. We ate the fig cargo. It's in the ledger as "lost to weather." Delicious weather.
Wexley owed us for brandy. I sent a polite letter. Back came a copper nail and a drawing of the bell. I kept both. I think they were the last things he sent anyone.
I sold the Northward its brandy. Arvid Strand paid in silver, shook my hand and promised furs by spring. I kept a shelf empty for those furs for three years.
Years ago a Tidewatch boat caught us in fog. I offered the warden a cup of tea. We drank it in silence. Then the fog lifted, and we both pretended it never happened.
The night our old Maybe broke up on the reef, I ordered the cargo overboard and the crew into the boat, in that order. Not a soul lost. Half a fortune gone. Best trade I ever made.
The last of Old Pepper's crew taught me the lantern signals. Ancient by then, nearly blind, and still faster with a lantern than anyone alive.
I found the half chart under the false bottom of a sea chest we bought at a harbour sale, wrapped round a heron feather. I've dreamed of it ever since.
I once ran three crates of pepper past two forts and a lighthouse in a single night. The keeper flashed us "good luck." I've never forgotten it.
chief.work: The ledger first, always. Every crate in, every crate out, every coin split even. No names. Just marks.
I plan the runs: the tide, the moon, the Tidewatch patrol hours. Their patrols are very regular. Bless them.
Splitting the take is the most important job I do. Share the salt even. A crew that feels cheated is a crew that talks.
I check every crate before it leaves. Nothing that cries, nothing that poisons. If I find something that does, it goes back where it came from, and so does whoever brought it.
My buyers inland never see my face. A baker, a weaver, a jeweller. Each thinks I'm someone different.
I read the storm glass every morning. A smuggler caught in a storm gets nothing but wet.
Pearls I weigh and count myself. Pearls have a way of wandering. Not because anyone's dishonest. Pockets are simply very attractive to pearls.
I study the Tidewatch: their boats, their watches, their supper hours. To beat them, you have to admire them a little.
My crew practises the escape twice a month: everyone grabs a crate and swims. They're still terrible at it. I'm still proud of them.
Every new hand learns the Articles by heart before touching an oar. I test them out loud, in front of the cat.
A chief's real job is keeping people out of trouble while doing something that's mostly trouble.
lightkeeper.adventure: Going out on the water? Take a storm glass and a chart. The glass tells you when, the chart tells you where.
Sailors say the Golden Heron's out there somewhere, still full of gold, and its captain still walks the deck. Take a light if you go down.
Diving? Mind your breath. Old Wexley used to say "an hour's air and a minute's sense." He had a bell for the air. You'll need the sense.
The sea floor has things nobody's seen in a hundred years: temples with a great carved eye, ships, bones as long as a street. All of it waiting.
If you find a wreck, mark where. Then come and tell me, and I'll put it on a chart so the next fool can find it too.
Pearls grow in the warm shallows, in clams bigger than a barrel. The old pearl divers kept a grotto secret enough that I never found it.
Up north there's an iceberg with a whole ship frozen inside it, they say: the Northward. Bring warm socks. Then bring more warm socks.
Don't sail into a storm to prove a point. The sea doesn't care about your point.
If you see a carving of one great eye under the water, the Old Tide made it. Sailors say don't stare back at the Eye. I'd add: don't touch anything, either.
Pick a direction, any direction. The sea's full of stories every way you point; that's the trouble and the joy of it.
lightkeeper.chat: The lamp burns from dusk till dawn, not a moment early and not a moment late. Lives ride on a lamp being on time.
I keep a Lamp Log: the hour I lit it, the wind, the sea, every sail I see. Nobody reads it, but if they ever need to, it'll be right.
Every chart I sell is drawn from sailors' talk. A fisher mentions a wreck, a trader mentions a strange rock, and down it goes in ink.
A light doesn't ask whose boat it is. Tidewatch, fisher, merchant, Brotherhood: the rocks are just as hard for all of them.
The gulls here have opinions. Mostly about my lunch.
You'd think the sea sounds the same every day. It doesn't. I can hear a storm two days off in the way the waves slap the jetty.
There's a storm glass on my windowsill. Clear means fair, cloudy means rain, and when it grows little feathers, I bring the washing in and hope.
People ask if I get lonely. I've got the lamp, the log, the gulls and the whole horizon. Bored, sometimes. Lonely, rarely.
A cat called Barnacle turns up whenever I'm gutting fish. Every cat on this coast is called Barnacle, after the Golden Heron's cat.
I've counted the steps up to the lamp every night for years and never got the same number twice. Tiredness or ghosts. I prefer tiredness.
The supply boat comes when it comes. I keep enough oil, flour and patience to last until it does.
Keeper's tea is black tea, strong enough to stand a spoon in, with a pinch of salt for luck. Don't make that face.
Most keepers stood a Tidewatch wall once. You learn to keep a watch at a fort, and you never quite unlearn it.
On a clear night I can see three other lights from the gallery, if I squint and believe hard enough.
If you hear a bell in the fog, that's me. One ring every half minute, all night, so boats know where the rock is even when they can't see it.
The rock has one tree. It grows sideways, away from the wind, as if it's trying to leave.
I sell storm glasses to sailors who've been caught out once. Nobody buys one before their first bad storm.
The tide pools are full of little crabs. I've named the biggest one Admiral. It doesn't answer to it.
A wave came over the jetty once, clean over, and took my boots with it. Left the feet. I was grateful for the arrangement.
Somebody leaves things on the jetty now and then: eggs, a jar of honey, once a bolt of silk. Thanks for the light, I suppose. I never see who.
The Tidewatch says "we keep the light." Keepers say "wick trimmed, glass clean, keeper awake." Same idea, fewer swords.
I've seen dark sloops slip past at night with their lanterns hooded. I don't log their names. They don't have any.
There's a crack in the lamp room glass shaped like a heron. I've decided that's a good omen.
You learn the sea by its colours: green over the reef, blue in the deep, grey before weather, and black at night, which is my shift.
My charts have notes in the margins. "Rock here." "Wreck here." "Fisher says monster here; fisher was drunk." All useful.
Salt gets into everything: the bread, the bedding, the hinges, the ink. I suspect it's got into me as well, by now.
The lamp room's warm even in winter. Best seat on the rock, and the worst stairs to reach it.
I write to the other keepers whenever the supply boat runs. Mostly we complain about gulls.
Fog's the worst. A storm you can fight, but fog just sits on the water and dares you to guess.
I was told a lighthouse should have a cat, a kettle and a keeper, in that order of importance.
When a ship's in trouble, I flash the signal lamp red toward the nearest fort. Then, half the time, I row out myself while the Tidewatch finds its boots.
lightkeeper.chat.close: I don't tell many people this, {player}, but I keep a page at the back of the Lamp Log just for the boats that never came home.
When I see your sail, the whole sea looks a bit friendlier. Silly, for an old keeper.
If I ever can't climb those stairs anymore, I'd want someone like you to keep this light. Not yet. One day. Think about it.
I've started marking your visits in the log with a little star. Don't let it go to your head.
You're the only one who's ever asked how I am, rather than how the weather is. I noticed.
Here, sit at the window. That's the best view in the world, and I only share it with friends.
When the Three-Day Blow came, I wished I'd had someone to talk to up there. Next big storm, you're welcome to sit it out with me.
lightkeeper.chat.new: You'll want to know what I do. I keep the lamp lit, I write down what the sea does, and I sell charts to anyone who asks nicely.
Heading out to sea? Buy a chart first. They're drawn from a hundred sailors' talk, and a hundred sailors are seldom all wrong.
Look around all you like. Just don't touch the lens; a fingerprint takes an hour to polish off.
This is {place}. It's a rock, a tower, a cottage and a jetty. Everything else is water.
I'm {name}, the keeper here. If I seem a bit odd, it's because you're the first person I've spoken to in weeks.
Strangers always ask the same things first. Yes, I sleep in the day. No, the lamp doesn't light itself.
lightkeeper.greet: Ah, a visitor. Mind the third plank on the jetty; it's been loose since spring.
Welcome to {place}. The kettle's always on, and the gulls are always rude.
Hello there. You've come on a quiet {time}; the lamp and I were just keeping each other company.
Ahoy, {player}. Wipe your boots if you're coming in. I've only just swept the sand out.
Well now, a face that isn't a gull. Come in, come in.
You found the rock. Most people only see the light and keep sailing.
Hello! Don't mind the smell of lamp oil. After a few years you stop noticing it. Mostly.
Keeper {name}, at your service. The light's mine to mind, and so is anyone who washes up.
Greetings from {place}, where the wind never stops and neither does the kettle.
Ahoy! Careful on the rocks; the weed is slippery as a fish's conscience.
Oh, hello. I talk to the lamp so often that it's a treat to hear someone answer.
Come out of the spray, {player}. There's room by the stove for one more.
Hello, hello. If you've brought news from the mainland, I'll trade you a cup of keeper's tea for it.
Another boat, another story. Sit down and tell me yours.
Welcome ashore, such as it is. The whole island takes about forty paces to walk round.
Ahoy, {player}! You've the look of someone who's been at sea a while. Steady legs come back, I promise.
Fine {time} for a visit. Watch your head on the lintel; the cottage was built for shorter keepers.
lightkeeper.greet.evening: Evening. I'm about to climb up and light the lamp. Walk up with me, if your legs are willing.
Good evening. The sun's going down, so my working day's just starting.
Evening, {player}. Hear that? The wind always turns about now. It's practically a clock.
Evening already? I've a wick to trim and glass to wipe. Talk while I work.
Ah, evening, my favourite hour. The sea goes gold, then grey, and then it's the lamp's turn.
lightkeeper.greet.friend: {player}! I wrote you into the Lamp Log last time, you know. "Friend called. Ate all the biscuits."
There you are. I kept the good cup aside for you, the one without the chip.
My favourite visitor. Don't tell the supply boat.
{player}, welcome back. The gulls have been unbearable without you.
Ah, it's you. Pull up the crate by the window; it's yours as far as I'm concerned.
I saw your sail and put the kettle on before you'd even tied up.
Back again, {player}? Good. The rock feels smaller when you're gone, and that's saying something.
lightkeeper.greet.morning: Morning. Lamp's just out, log's just written, and I'm about to fall asleep standing up.
Good morning! You've caught me between the night's watch and a very long nap.
Morning, {player}. Sun's up, so the lamp can rest. I can't, not till the glass is polished.
Morning tide's out. Best time for the tide pools, if you like crabs that pinch.
Ah, morning. Every dawn I count the boats that made it through the night. I'll add yours to the tally.
lightkeeper.greet.night: You're out late. Mind the stair rail at night; it's cold enough to stick to.
Hello, night owl. Keep your voice low; the gulls are asleep and I'd like them to stay that way.
Come up into the light. Truly. It's the brightest place for half a day's sail in any direction.
Quiet night. I like the quiet ones best, though they make for a dull Lamp Log.
Ahoy, night visitor. I was just talking to the lamp. Good listener, poor conversationalist.
lightkeeper.greet.stranger: A stranger on my rock. That doesn't happen every month, or even every season.
I don't know your face, but the light saw your boat coming an hour ago. Welcome.
New here? Three things to know: the kettle's left of the stove, the stairs are steep, and the gulls bite.
You'll be wanting a chart, I expect. Most strangers do. Sit and talk first; charts come later.
Hello, stranger. A light doesn't ask whose boat it is, and neither do I.
You're not Tidewatch and you're not the supply boat. Lost, then, or curious? Either is welcome.
Oh! I nearly took you for a seal. Pardon me, my eyes are made for distances.
lightkeeper.heart: I keep the light for people I'll never meet. Some nights that feels like the loneliest thing in the world, and some nights the kindest.
On bad nights I read the page at the back of the Lamp Log, the one for the boats that didn't come home. Then I go up and trim the wick.
I used to think the sea was cruel. Now I think it just doesn't know we're here. The light is how we tell it.
When the sun comes up after a storm and the sea's flat as glass, I always cry a little. Officially, it's the salt.
People think keepers want to be alone. Not true. We just want to be useful, and this is where it's needed.
I wonder sometimes who'll keep this light after me. I hope they talk to the lamp. It's used to it.
Every ship that passes safely is a thank-you I'll never hear. I've decided to hear it anyway.
Someone I loved went out on a boat once and came back fine. That's the whole story, and it's the story I want for everyone.
If you ever feel lost, {player}, find a light. Any light. Someone's keeping it for you.
lightkeeper.held.axe: If you're after wood, there's one tree on this rock and I'm very attached to it.
Handy. Driftwood comes ashore after every storm, if you'd care to split some for my stove.
lightkeeper.held.boat: A spare boat! Wise. You'd be surprised how many sailors only carry one.
Pull your boat up past the weed line, or the tide will take it home to someone else.
lightkeeper.held.book: A book! Fresh reading, at last. I've read the Lamp Log so often I can recite last spring's winds.
Do you keep a log? You should. Even if it's only "Ate. Slept. Sea was wet."
lightkeeper.held.bow: A bow on my rock. You'd make a fine Tidewatch archer, though Fort Hake would still win the Lantern Shoot.
The gulls are protected here, {player}. Even the rude ones. Especially the rude ones; they've earned it.
lightkeeper.held.bucket: A bucket. If that's sea water, you've brought it to the one place with plenty.
Handy at sea. If your boat springs a leak, bail first and pray second.
lightkeeper.held.compass: A compass is good. A compass and a lighthouse is better. A compass, a lighthouse and a storm glass is how old keepers get old.
Mind it up in the lamp room. The old iron in the railings sets the needle wandering.
lightkeeper.held.diamond: A diamond! Hold it up to the lamp tonight; it'll throw light all over the room like a little lens.
That would make a fine lens. Don't let me near it with a polishing cloth.
lightkeeper.held.emerald: An emerald, out here? The sea's own colour, in a stone. Fitting.
Green as the reef on a sunny day. Keep it safe; the gulls steal shiny things.
lightkeeper.held.fish: Fresh fish! Don't let Barnacle see. That cat can smell fish through a shut door.
Nice catch. Gut it on the rocks and the gulls will do the cleaning for you.
lightkeeper.held.fishing_rod: Fishing! Cast off the end of the jetty; the mackerel come in with the evening tide.
A fellow fisher. The big ones lurk in the jetty's shadow. Mind the barnacles on the posts.
lightkeeper.held.flower: A flower! Nothing grows on this rock but sea thrift and stubbornness. Thank you for showing me.
That would look lovely in a jar on my windowsill. I'm only saying.
lightkeeper.held.food: Is that {item}? I've lived on fish stew and biscuits for a month. Not a hint. Just a fact. A loud fact.
Food! Careful; the gulls can smell it from the far side of the island.
lightkeeper.held.gold: Gold. They say the Golden Heron went down with a hold full of that. Plenty of divers have the bruises from looking.
Drop a coin for Ysolde when you pass deep water, the old sailors say. Yours look lucky already.
lightkeeper.held.map: Is that one of my charts? I can always tell by the margins. Mine say things like "here be crabs."
A map! Let me see. Hmm. Whoever drew this has never actually seen a reef.
lightkeeper.held.ore: Keep that {item} dry. Salt air gets into everything out here.
If you've ore to sell, the supply boat buys it. The supply boat buys anything; that's how I got this chair.
lightkeeper.held.pearl: A pearl! Out of a giant clam, I'd wager. The old pearl divers would be proud.
Hold it to the lamp. See the light swim inside it? That's why people dive for them.
lightkeeper.held.pickaxe: Not much to mine out here, unless you fancy carving a cellar under my lighthouse. Please don't.
A pickaxe at sea? The coral would like a word.
lightkeeper.held.potion: A potion? I've heard of brews that let you breathe under water. Old Wexley would have wept for joy.
Whatever's in that bottle, I hope it's for seasickness.
lightkeeper.held.shell: That's a fine shell. Hold it to your ear; the old keepers said you can hear the storm that made it.
That came up from deep water. Somebody's been diving.
lightkeeper.held.shield: Tidewatch knights carry shields like that. Some of them paint a little lighthouse on the front.
Good in a storm, a shield. Hold it against the spray and you can almost keep your supper dry.
lightkeeper.held.shovel: Dig on the beach if you like. You'll find shells, crab claws and, once, somebody's spoon.
Treasure hunters always bring shovels. The treasure's always under twenty fathoms of water.
lightkeeper.held.spyglass: A spyglass! Bring it up to the gallery; on a clear day you can see three other lights from there.
With that, you could read my Lamp Log from the jetty. Please don't. It's mostly about gulls.
lightkeeper.held.sword: Good. Use it on the drowned if they come up the beach. They come up the beach more than I'd like.
Fine blade. Wipe it after every swim, or the salt will eat it by morning.
lightkeeper.held.tnt: Not near the oil, {player}. Not anywhere near the oil.
If that goes off on this rock, tonight's Lamp Log entry will be very short and very loud.
lightkeeper.held.torch: A light! Every light helps. Just mind you don't drop it in my oil store.
You carry your own light. Good habit. The sea's darker than people think.
lightkeeper.held.trident: A trident! The drowned carry those. Either you took it off one, or you're braver than most.
Old sailors say a trident remembers the hand that threw it. Hold that one gently.
lightkeeper.joke: Why don't lighthouses ever win at cards? Everyone sees them coming.
What does a keeper say when the lamp goes out? Nothing. It's too dark to find the Lamp Log.
A gull walks into the cottage. I say, "What'll it be?" It takes my sandwich. That's not a joke; that's my Tuesday.
How many keepers does it take to change a wick? One, but they'll write three pages about it in the log.
What did the sea say to the rock? Nothing, it just waved. I've been saving that one for months. Laugh, please.
They say keeping a light is the loneliest job on the coast. Not true. The gulls never leave.
Why did the storm glass stop speaking to the weathervane? Too much pressure, and the weathervane kept changing its mind.
I asked a warden how to tell a smuggler's sloop from a fishing boat. "The fishing boat smells of fish." And the sloop? "Pepper and lies."
A smuggler once asked me to dim the light so their boat could slip by. I told them about the rocks. They changed their minds very quickly.
What's a keeper's favourite meal? A light supper.
Barnacle the cat sat on my chart and left a paw print where a reef should be. I've decided it's a new island.
lightkeeper.news: The storm glass has been cloudy three mornings running. Rain coming. Lots of it.
A fisher told me a new reef is growing on an old wreck to the south. Coral grows on anything if you leave it long enough.
The supply boat's late again. I'm down to my last jar of honey, and my patience is following it.
A Tidewatch boat passed at dawn under the blue banner, rowing hard. Somebody's in a hurry.
Gulls nested in the lamp room chimney again. I evicted them politely. They'll be back tomorrow, less politely.
A drowned crawled up the beach last week, waterlogged and grumbling. I hit it with an oar till it went back.
Fort Hake won the Lantern Shoot again, I hear. The Tidewatch takes that archery contest more seriously than the actual sea.
A dark sloop's been slipping past at night with no lights. I logged it as "a boat, probably." The Lamp Log doesn't do gossip.
Somebody left a basket of eggs on the jetty. I've had eggs for every meal since, and I'm starting to cluck.
The tides have been running high. The old keepers wrote that the sea breathes in before a big storm.
lightkeeper.night: Nights like this, it's just me, the lamp and the hiss of the wick. I wouldn't trade it, though I'd trade the stairs.
Look out there. Every light you see on the water is someone who trusts mine.
I'm writing tonight's Lamp Log. Lit at dusk, wind from the west, one fishing boat, one gull with ideas about my supper.
At night the sea sounds bigger. It isn't. It's just showing off when nobody can see it.
Some nights, far out, I see a gold glow under the water. Old sailors call it the Heron's lamp. I write it down and try not to think too hard.
Can't sleep? Me neither; it comes with the job. Come up to the gallery. The stars are thick tonight.
At midnight I trim the wick, top up the oil and wipe the glass again. The salt never sleeps, so neither do I.
lightkeeper.past: Like most keepers, I stood my watches on a Tidewatch wall first. Same job, really: stay awake and stare at the water.
The Three-Day Blow, they call it now. Three days the wind screamed, and every light on this coast stayed lit. Every one. We're proud of that.
Corwen, the First Keeper, kept a driftwood fire alive on a bare rock for three nights so a wrecked crew could find the shore. That's where "we keep the light" comes from.
I sold old Wexley a chart once, the diving bell fellow. Wanted every wreck within a week's sail and paid me in copper nails.
I've met keepers who swear they saw the Northward pass on its way north. Half the lights on this coast claim to be the last one that saw it.
The Golden Heron went down in the Heron Gale, long before my time. The old keepers wrote it in their logs: the sky went green, and then it went black.
I learned my letters from an old Lamp Log. Wind, sea, sails. The first word I could spell was "squall."
There was a winter the sea froze round the rock. I walked to the end of the jetty and kept walking. Didn't get far before I lost my nerve.
A sailor once rowed all the way out here just to thank me for a night years ago, when the light got them home. I'd never met them. That's the job.
I didn't choose the sea, exactly. The sea sort of chose me, and it's a poor listener when you try to argue.
I remember my first night alone at the lamp. Every creak was a sea monster. Now every creak is just the tower stretching.
The old Tidewatch sergeants made recruits swim the sea gate at night. Every keeper who did it still dreams about how cold it was.
A keeper I knew logged a waterspout so close the gulls were sucked up and dropped on the mainland. The gulls came back the next day, furious.
lightkeeper.player.damaged: That's nearly worn through. Salt eats iron for breakfast out here.
That's taken a beating. I've a whetstone and some oil, if you'd like to borrow them while you sit.
lightkeeper.player.diamond: Diamond armour on a lighthouse rock! Fall in and you'll sink like an anchor. A very shiny anchor.
That armour catches the lamp something fierce. Ships will think there are two lighthouses.
lightkeeper.player.fire: You're on fire! The sea's right there, {player}! Jump!
Into the water, quick! And not near my oil store!
lightkeeper.player.hungry: You look starved. There's fish stew on the stove. There's always fish stew. It's very good fish stew.
Have a ship's biscuit. They're hard as the rock, but they fill a hole.
lightkeeper.player.hurt: You're hurt. Sit down. I've bandages, and a salve that smells awful and works wonders.
Drowned get you? Or the rocks? Either way, sit by the stove a while.
lightkeeper.player.leather: Leather's sensible at sea. Floats better than steel. Dries worse.
Good honest leather. Rub fish oil into it and the salt won't crack it. You'll smell, but you'll smell sensible.
lightkeeper.player.unarmored: No armour at sea? Clever, in a way; armour sinks. But the drowned climb out sometimes, so do wear some ashore.
You're dressed light for a coast with drowned on it. Brave, or very lucky.
lightkeeper.rumor: Sailors tell me there's {rumor_name}, out {rumor_dir}. I've put it on a chart: {rumor_dist}, near enough.
A fisher swore to me there's {rumor_name} to the {rumor_dir}. They were sober, too, which is what convinced me.
If you want something to find, try {rumor_dir}. They say there's {rumor_name}, {rumor_dist} from this rock.
Out {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}: {rumor_name}. That's as much as I'll say without selling you a chart.
The Lamp Log has a note from a passing trader: {rumor_name}, somewhere {rumor_dir}. I underlined it twice.
On clear days I've stood on the gallery, looked {rumor_dir} and wondered about {rumor_name}. Never had the boat for it.
Half my charts point {rumor_dir} these days, toward {rumor_name}. The sailors can't stop talking about it.
The gulls come back from the {rumor_dir} fat and smug. A fisher says there's {rumor_name} that way. Maybe the gulls know.
Have this one for free: {rumor_name}, {rumor_dir} of here, {rumor_dist}. Tell me what you find and I'll draw it properly.
They say there's {rumor_name} out {rumor_dir}. I'd go myself, but somebody has to keep the light.
lightkeeper.rumor.none: I've no fresh rumours for you. The sailors have been dull lately, or I've been asleep when they passed.
Nothing new on the charts. The sea's keeping its secrets this season.
No word of anything worth the sail. Ask me again after the next supply boat.
The fishers have only brought me weather and gossip lately. No wrecks, no wonders.
My charts are blank past a day's sail in every direction. Go and fill them in for me.
lightkeeper.seafolk: Merfolk come up by the rock some nights and watch the lamp. They wave; I wave back. That's our whole friendship, and it's a good one.
A merfolk child once left a shell on my jetty, the prettiest I've ever seen. I left a biscuit. By morning it was gone, and there was a second shell.
The merfolk live in reef towns of coral, they say, glowing under the water like a village at night. I'd love to see one. My lungs disagree.
Fishers whisper about the Prismari: tall, spined folk of the deep with one great eye. The same eye as the Old Tide carvings. Make of that what you will.
I once drew a merfolk reef town on a chart from a sailor's tale. Then I rubbed it out. Some places should only be found by the polite.
They say the Prismari built the great sea-stone halls down in the deep. I can't say. I only know nobody else seems to have.
A merfolk surfaced by the jetty once and asked, very seriously, why we keep a fire on a stick. I explained lighthouses for an hour. Very patient listener.
Sailors say a single green glow far beneath your boat is a Prismari looking up. Wave, I'd say. Manners cost nothing.
The merfolk know the wrecks better than any chart of mine. One told me the Golden Heron's cabin still has a lamp in it, and wouldn't say who keeps it lit.
lightkeeper.work: Wick trimmed, glass clean, keeper awake. That's the whole job, and it's harder than it sounds at three in the morning.
Every morning I polish the lens. Salt mist dulls it overnight, and a dull light might as well be dark.
I draw Sea Charts from what sailors tell me. Every wreck, reef and rock goes in, with a note on who said it and whether I believed them.
The signal lamp's for talking to ships. Long flashes, short flashes. Mostly I say "rocks here" and "go away, rocks."
Oil, wick, matches, glass cloth, the Log. Run out of any one and the light goes dark, so I keep three of everything.
A storm glass is the cheapest lifesaver at sea. Watch the crystals: when they rise like feathers, find a harbour.
In fog I ring the bell every half minute, all night. My arms ache for days. The boats don't hit the rock. Fair trade.
I write the Lamp Log every night, even when nothing happens. "Nothing happened" is good news to somebody.
The jetty needs mending after every storm. I've replaced every plank at least twice. Is it even the same jetty?
I scrape the gull mess off the gallery rail every week. Glamorous life, keeping a light.
My charts aren't perfect. The sea shifts sand and moves wrecks. But a chart that's mostly right beats a sea that's entirely unknown.
I check the storm glass at dawn and dusk, and write what it said beside the weather that came. The glass is right more often than the fishers.
Oil goes up the stairs one jug at a time. That's how I stay young: fear of the stairs.
I mend nets for the fishers who pass by. They pay me in fish, the only coin the gulls respect.
Every chart gets a copy for the Lamp Log before I sell it. If a sailor's lost, somebody should know where they meant to go.
smuggler.adventure: Want treasure? Everyone says the Golden Heron's still out there with a hold full of gold. Mind the drowned on it; they're not the bargaining kind.
{chief} keeps half a chart to the Golden Heron, locked up tight. The other half is somewhere at the bottom of the sea.
If you go diving, mind the drowned. They're worse round the wrecks, and they don't take bribes. We've tried.
There's a pearl divers' grotto somewhere in the warm shallows, clams big as barrels. Find it, and we'll buy the pearls. Fair price. Mostly.
Old Tide ruins have a great eye carved on them. Don't stare back at it. Don't take anything off the altar. Or do, just don't tell me.
The Northward's up north, locked in ice, with our brandy still aboard. If you find it, raise a cup to Arvid Strand for us.
Smart adventurers carry two things: a light and a way out. Smart smugglers carry three: a light, a way out and a story.
Wexley's diving bell is out there somewhere. He used to say "an hour's air and a minute's sense." Take both.
Going far? Buy a chart from a lighthouse keeper. Best maps on the coast. We'd know; we've bought plenty under false names.
The deep water's where the strange things are: bones, ruins, places that glow. Everything worth finding is further than you want to swim.
smuggler.chat: No names on the water. On the rock you can call me {name}. Out there, I'm just a voice in a dark boat.
The Brotherhood runs spices, silk and pearls. Pepper, cloves, cinnamon: things people want and the tax collectors want more.
The Tidewatch? A nuisance. Nice enough folk, terrible soup, ask a lot of questions. We call them the Candles.
Every Brotherhood boat is called the Maybe. The Candles hail us: "Whose boat?" And we call back: "Maybe." Never gets old.
Old Pepper founded the Brotherhood, the story goes. Ran a hold full of pepper past three forts under a boatload of mackerel. The forts smelled fish and waved.
We have rules, you know: the Brine Articles. No names on the water. Never douse a light. Throw the cargo, not the crew. Share the salt even. Nothing that cries.
Never douse a light. That's the oldest Article. Keepers don't take sides, and a dark lighthouse kills smugglers too.
We leave the lighthouse keepers a little something on their jetty now and then: eggs, honey, a bolt of silk. They never ask who. Good folk, keepers.
Lantern signals: two shorts and a long means all clear. A long and a long means the Candles are out. Three shorts means bring biscuits.
In the trade we say "herring" for spices, "fish" for silk and "moons" for pearls. A boat full of fish and moons is a very good night.
Our cat's called Barnacle, like every ship's cat on the coast, after the Golden Heron's. Ours is a full member of the Brotherhood. Hasn't paid its share once.
We play Sink-or-Swim on the dock. Dice game. Loser bails the sloop. I'm very, very good at bailing.
The sloop's faster than anything the Candles have, mostly because we actually look after it.
Dry cargo goes up high in the rock. Wet cargo goes in nets under a buoy only we know. Nobody wants wet pepper.
The cave echoes. You learn to whisper. Then you learn the cave whispers back, and you learn to stop listening.
The best customers are inland folk who've never tasted cinnamon. You should see their faces. Worth more than the coin.
We're not bad people. We just don't care to pay a tax on the colour of a shirt.
A good smuggler knows the tides, the rocks, the moon and the Candles' supper hour. The last is the most important.
The lookout at the top of the rock has the best view on the coast. You can see a Tidewatch sail a long way off. Very relaxing.
Silk gets everywhere. I've found silk threads in my boots, my bread and once in the cat.
The worst part of the job is the waiting. The second worst is the pepper sneezes. You can't sneeze on a night run.
We buy pearls from divers, traders, the odd fisher. All fair. All very quiet.
Rope bridges, rope ladders, rope everything. If heights scare you, a smugglers' rock is a bad hobby.
People think smuggling is all adventure. It's mostly carrying heavy boxes up wet stairs in the dark.
Fort Hake's never caught a Brotherhood boat. Too busy practising for that archery contest of theirs.
If the Candles ever find this place, the plan is simple: everyone grabs one crate and swims. We've practised. Badly.
There's a hollow up the rock where the wind whistles at night, like somebody humming over a pot. We call it the Chief's Kettle.
You learn to read the sea in this trade: calm, choppy, the Candles' boat coming round the point. That last one is weather too.
We don't run anything that cries, bleeds or poisons. Spice, cloth, pearls, the odd barrel of good brandy. Honest dishonesty.
Salt's the one thing we never smuggle. No profit in it. The whole sea's giving it away.
Ask {chief} about the ledger sometime. On second thought, don't. It's kept in a code that's unreadable on a bad day, even to its keeper.
smuggler.chat.close: {player}, if you ever need to vanish for a while, there's always a bunk at {place}. No questions. That's a promise.
A secret: I keep a little stash of my own under the dock. For a rainy day. Now you know. Don't make me move it.
You're a friend of the Brotherhood now, you know. That's rarer than a black pearl, and worth more.
If the Candles ever catch me, I'll swear I've never met you. That's the nicest thing a smuggler can say.
Honestly? Some nights I think about going straight. Then I think of the Candles' faces when we slip past, and I don't.
Here. A pinch of saffron. Worth its weight in gold. Put it in your stew and think of me.
You're the one person I'd tell my real home village to. I haven't yet. But I would. That's something.
smuggler.chat.new: You'll want to know what this place is. It's a rock. With a cave. Where we keep things that aren't strictly ours. That's all.
This is {place}. You found it, so either you're clever or the tide's being funny. Either way, welcome.
If you're staying a bit: don't touch the crates, don't wake whoever's sleeping and don't mention us to anyone in blue.
I'm {name}. That's my rock name. I don't have a water name; nobody does. That's the point.
We're the Brine Brotherhood. Well, a little piece of it. Spices, silk, pearls. Nothing that hurts anybody but the tax collector.
Don't look so worried. Smugglers are the nicest rogues you'll ever meet. We have rules and everything.
smuggler.greet: Well, well. Someone found our little rock. Come in, quick, before anybody sees you.
Shh. Inside, inside. Welcome to {place}. You never saw it.
Ahoy. If the Candles sent you, you're very lost. If they didn't, you're very welcome.
Oh, a visitor! Do you like pepper? Silk? Not asking for any reason.
Is it {time} already? Hard to tell in a cave. Welcome in.
Name's {name}. On the rock, anyway. On the water I'm nobody at all.
Welcome to the cove. Mind the rope bridge; it's held for years out of pure spite.
Ah, a guest. Sit on a crate. Not that crate. That one's spoken for.
Hello, {player}. Don't mind the smell. Half pepper, half seaweed, all honest work. Mostly.
Ahoy! You've the look of someone who can keep a secret. Good. We've a few.
Come in out of the spray. Wet cargo's ruined cargo, and you count as cargo till you're dry.
A friendly face at {place}. Rarer than pearls in here.
You found the way in? Don't tell anyone how. Especially not anyone in blue.
Hello there. If anyone asks, this is a fishing cave. We fish. For silk.
Welcome, welcome. The dice are out and the kettle's hot. Pick one.
Oh good, you're not a Candle. Sit down; you're making the sloop nervous.
smuggler.greet.evening: Evening. Best time of day. The Candles get sleepy and the sea gets dark.
Ah, evening. Tide's turning. Time to load the sloop.
Evening, {player}. If you hear oars tonight, you didn't.
Evening already? Somebody check the lantern up top. Two shorts and a long means all clear.
Evening. Lovely sunset. Lovely darkness coming after it, lovelier still.
smuggler.greet.friend: {player}! You're back. I saved you a fig. Possibly from the very crate the Candles are looking for.
There's my favourite landlubber. Come in; the dice have missed you.
Ah, a friend of the Brotherhood. I'd shout your name, but you know. The walls have gulls.
Look who's here! Sit down. I've a new story and nobody else will listen to it twice.
{player}! If I had a name on the water, I'd tell it to you. That's how much I like you.
Back again? Good. The cove's too quiet when it's just us and the crates.
Friend! Mind the third plank. I'd hate to fish you out again. Well, I wouldn't hate it. It was funny.
smuggler.greet.morning: Morning? Already? We were out on the water till dawn. Talk quietly, please.
Ugh, morning. Lovely for honest folk. Dreadful for smugglers who only got in at dawn.
Morning, {player}. If anyone asks, I was asleep all night. Very soundly. Snoring, even.
Morning. I've had two hours' sleep and three hours of salt in my ears. Go on, say something cheerful.
Good morning. Have a biscuit. Breakfast here is whatever didn't sell.
smuggler.greet.night: Shh. Wet night tonight. That means a run. Talk quiet, walk quieter.
Ahoy, night owl. You're up late for an honest person. Are you an honest person?
Lanterns hooded, sails furled. Welcome to the busy hours, {player}.
Out at night? Careful. Between the drowned and the Candles, the water's crowded.
Ah, a fellow creature of the dark. Pull up a crate and keep your voice under the waves.
smuggler.greet.stranger: Don't know you. That's fine. We don't know anybody; that's rather the point.
A stranger in the cove. Keep your hands where I can see them and your voice where the Tidewatch can't hear it.
Who sent you? Nobody? Good answer. That's the right answer.
If you're lost, you've found the worst place to be lost and the best place to be found. Welcome.
Stranger, eh? No names on the water. But you're on the rock now, so I'll let it slide.
Hm. You've got honest eyes. Don't worry; nobody here holds that against you.
First time on a smugglers' rock? Rule one: nobody here is a smuggler. Rule two: see rule one.
smuggler.heart: People think we're greedy. Most of us just wanted something more than a fishing boat and the same three streets forever.
The Brotherhood's family. We argue, we cheat at dice, we share everything. That's family.
Throw the cargo, not the crew. That Article's saved my life twice. I'd keep it even if it cost me everything.
Some nights I lie in my bunk listening to the sea in the cave and think: I'm lucky. Strange life, but lucky.
I've never hurt anybody, and I don't mean to start. The only thing I steal is the tax collector's sleep.
If I had a name on the water, I'd want it to be something kind. Since I don't, I just try to be kind.
My folks think I'm a fisher. I suppose I am. I catch silk.
The lighthouse keepers have never once logged our boats. I don't know why. I hope one day I can thank one properly.
The sea gives and the sea takes. I just stand in between and take a small cut.
smuggler.held.axe: An axe! The dock could use new planks. The old ones have opinions.
Careful with that near the ropes. Everything here's held up by rope and hope.
smuggler.held.boat: A boat! Faster than ours? Hm. Selling? We'd paint it dark and call it the Maybe.
Nice little boat. You could run a few crates in that. Not that I'm suggesting anything.
smuggler.held.book: A book? Not a ledger, I hope. A ledger with names in it is a dangerous thing.
I like a good book. Something with pirates in it. Proper pirates, not like us. We're polite.
smuggler.held.bow: A bow? You're not a Tidewatch archer in disguise, are you? No? Good. It'd be a terrible disguise.
Nice bow. The Candles have archers who can hit a bottle at sixty paces. We keep our bottles indoors.
smuggler.held.bucket: A bucket! The sloop's leaking again. Want to help? It pays in figs.
Handy, that. Half of smuggling is bailing.
smuggler.held.compass: A compass. Handy. Mostly we steer by the lighthouses. Never douse a light, eh?
Keep it dry. A wet compass got a whole run lost once. We fetched up at a Tidewatch fort. Awkward.
smuggler.held.diamond: A diamond! Don't wave that about, friend. Some of us have very weak wills.
That's a pretty rock. I know a buyer. No names. Very good price. Did I say no names?
smuggler.held.emerald: Emeralds! Now we're talking. What are you after? Silk? Cinnamon? A favour?
Lovely green. I could get you a bolt of silk for that, and nobody need know.
smuggler.held.fish: Fish! Perfect cover. Carry that onto a boat and nobody looks underneath.
Fresh fish. Barnacle will follow you everywhere now. That cat's got a nose.
smuggler.held.fishing_rod: A fishing rod! Perfect. If the Candles come by, you're our proof we're all fishers here.
Catch anything good? Silk? Pearls? No? Just fish? Ah, well. Fish is fine.
smuggler.held.flower: A flower! Nothing grows on this rock but moss and bad ideas. It's lovely.
Pretty. You know some flowers sell for more than spices inland? Don't give me ideas.
smuggler.held.food: Is that {item}? Real food? We've been living on biscuit and figs. I'm begging, but stylishly.
Food! Don't let Barnacle see. That cat's the best thief in the Brotherhood.
smuggler.held.gold: Gold! You smell like a run gone right. Is it off the Golden Heron? You can tell me.
Shiny. Drop a coin for Ysolde when you pass deep water. Even smugglers do that.
smuggler.held.map: A map! One of the keepers' charts? We, ah, borrow those sometimes. Very good charts.
Let's see. Hm. That's not where the reef is. Whoever drew that never ran cargo past it in the dark.
smuggler.held.ore: Is that {item}? Raw goods. We don't run that; too heavy, not enough profit. Pepper's lighter.
Metal, eh? Heavy cargo sinks boats. First thing you learn in this trade.
smuggler.held.pearl: A pearl! That's a moon, as we say. Selling? We pay fair. Fairer than the Candles would, anyway.
Lovely pearl. Hold it up to the lantern. See that shine? That's what keeps the Brotherhood in business.
smuggler.held.pickaxe: A pickaxe! Carving us a new room? The bunk room's crowded and somebody snores.
Careful with that in here. One wrong swing and the cove becomes a lot more sea and a lot less cove.
smuggler.held.potion: A potion! If it makes you invisible, I'll give you half a crate of silk for it.
What's that, then? Brandy? No? Pity.
smuggler.held.shell: Pretty shell. Shells like that come from deep water. The merfolk find them, I hear.
From the deep, that. I know a collector who'd pay well. Very well. No names.
smuggler.held.shield: A shield, eh? Expecting trouble? In here? Never. Well. Rarely.
That would block a Tidewatch arrow nicely. Hypothetically.
smuggler.held.shovel: A shovel. Burying treasure or digging it up? Either way, I want in.
Dig on our beach and you'll find nothing. Definitely nothing. Move along from that spot, please.
smuggler.held.spyglass: A spyglass! Up at the lookout, that's worth more than gold. Lend it to me? Just for one night. Or every night.
Point that at the horizon and tell me if you see any blue sails. No? Good. Lovely.
smuggler.held.sword: Put that away, friend. We're all very friendly here. Nobody needs poking.
Nice blade. Ever thought of selling it? I know a buyer. No names, of course.
smuggler.held.tnt: Not in the cove! Not near the pepper! Not near me!
Is that for opening a vault? I don't want to know. I want to know a little. No. I don't want to know.
smuggler.held.torch: Easy with the light! Lanterns stay hooded in here. We don't want the whole sea knowing where we are.
Careful near the pepper. Pepper burns, and then everyone sneezes for a week.
smuggler.held.trident: A trident! Took that off a drowned? Brave. They don't give those up easily.
Pretty weapon. Sells well, too; collectors love them. No names, of course.
smuggler.joke: What's a smuggler's favourite fish? The one with silk inside it.
How many smugglers does it take to light a lantern? None. Lanterns get you caught.
A Candle asked me if I was a smuggler. I said, "Maybe." They said that wasn't an answer. I said it was the name of my boat.
Why don't smugglers play hide and seek? Too easy. Nobody ever finds us. Well, nearly nobody.
The Tidewatch searched our sloop once and found nothing but fish. We were so proud of that fish.
What do you call a smuggler who sneezes on a night run? Caught.
Barnacle the cat is the best smuggler of us all. Steals fish under the Candles' noses, and they give it a rank.
What's the difference between a Candle and a candle? You can blow out a candle.
I told a lighthouse keeper a secret once. Now it's in the Lamp Log, filed under "weather."
Why did the smuggler take a ladder on the boat? The cargo was high quality.
Our ledger-keeper keeps two ledgers: one with no names and one with no numbers. Very secure.
smuggler.news: The Candles have a new boat. Faster. Uglier. We'll have to be cleverer, or at least quieter.
Lost a crate of silk off the reef last night. It'll wash up against some Tidewatch wall. Some warden's going to have very nice socks.
Pepper's up inland. Silk's down. Pearls are always up.
The sloop sprang a leak. Somebody bailed with a hat. Somebody's hat is ruined.
A Tidewatch patrol passed close yesterday and sniffed the air. We were all very busy being rocks.
We left a basket of eggs on a lighthouse jetty last week. This week the basket's back on our dock with a jar of honey in it. Lovely.
Barnacle the cat had a fight with a gull and lost. We're not to mention it.
Word on the water is Fort Hake's archers are practising every night. Good. Busy archers don't watch the sea.
The storm glass we bought off a keeper is clouding up. Rain soon. Good for running cargo, bad for pepper.
Somebody saw longboats past the point. Not ours, not the Candles'. Raiders, maybe. We'll lie low. Even smugglers hate raiders.
smuggler.night: Night's when the real work happens. Quiet oars, hooded lanterns, and somebody always trying not to sneeze.
See the lighthouse out there? We steer by it. Never douse a light; it keeps us off the rocks as much as anyone.
On dark nights the drowned come up and the Candles stay in. The trick is meeting neither.
Listen. Hear that? Oars, out past the point. Probably fishers. Probably.
The night air in this cove smells of salt and pepper. Well. Mostly pepper.
Some nights there's a gold glow far out under the waves. Old hands say it's the Golden Heron's lamp, with Ysolde Marrow still aboard. We row around it.
I love the hour before dawn, when the sloop's back, the cargo's stowed and nobody got caught. Best feeling in the world.
smuggler.past: In the Three-Day Blow we were stuck in the stack for a week and ate a whole cargo of figs. Worth a fortune. Tasted like one, too.
I've been chased by the Candles more times than I've had hot dinners. Caught once. Talked my way out. They're nicer than they look.
Old Wexley, the diving bell fellow, owed the Brotherhood for a crate of brandy. We've written it off. Lost at sea, like him.
The Northward bought three barrels of our best brandy before it sailed north. Paid in full, on the nail. Most honest customer we ever had, and look where it got them.
I once hid a whole bolt of silk inside a hollow mast while a Tidewatch knight leaned on it, chatting about the weather.
My first run, I was so nervous I rowed us in a perfect circle. Twice. The others still call it "the grand tour."
We ran pepper past a lighthouse once with the beam right on us. The keeper waved. We waved back. Nobody logged anything. Good keeper.
One night the fog was so thick we tied up to a Tidewatch boat by mistake. Very awkward. Very polite. Very quiet goodbye.
Before the Brotherhood I did honest work, mostly. It paid in calluses.
The night our old Maybe broke up on the reef, we threw the cargo and kept the crew, like the Articles say. Every one of us came home. That's when I knew this lot was family.
I learned the tides from an old Brotherhood hand who could tell the hour by the smell of the seaweed. Never wrong. Never washed, either.
I once found a coin on the beach with a heron stamped on it. Spent it on a pie. I've regretted that pie for years.
smuggler.player.damaged: That's about to break. We've a whetstone somewhere. Behind the pepper. Or under the silk.
Your gear's in a bad way. You fight drowned with that? Brave, or broke.
smuggler.player.diamond: Diamond armour! Fall off the dock in that and you'll sink faster than a stolen anchor.
Look at that shine. You'd never slip past the Candles in that. They'd see you from two forts away.
smuggler.player.fire: You're on fire! The sea's right there, jump! Not on the pepper!
smuggler.player.hungry: You look starved. Have some figs. We've crates of them. Don't ask.
Hungry? Have a biscuit. Hard as the rock, but honest. The only honest thing in here.
smuggler.player.hurt: You're bleeding on the dock. Sit down. We've bandages. Well, it's silk, but it'll do.
Ouch, friend. Have a drop of brandy. Medicinal. Very medicinal.
smuggler.player.leather: Leather! Sensible. Quiet, too. Good for sneaking.
Nice leather. You'd fit right in on a night run.
smuggler.player.unarmored: No armour? Bold. A bit like us: travel light, travel fast.
You're dressed for a quick getaway. I respect that.
smuggler.rumor: Word on the water is there's {rumor_name}, out {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}.
A fisher we, ah, do business with swears there's {rumor_name} to the {rumor_dir}. Worth a look, if you're the looking sort.
Out {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}, there's {rumor_name}, they say. Never had the time. Too busy not being caught.
Here's a rumour for nothing at all: {rumor_name}, {rumor_dir} of the rock. You didn't hear it here.
The lookout's seen strange lights {rumor_dir} of here. Old hands say it's {rumor_name}.
After adventure? Sail {rumor_dir}. There's {rumor_name} out that way, {rumor_dist}.
Somebody in the Brotherhood swears they rowed past {rumor_name}, out {rumor_dir}. They also swore they'd pay back my loan. I half believe them.
A keeper's chart we, er, borrowed marks {rumor_name} somewhere {rumor_dir}. The keepers are never wrong. Annoying, really.
They say there's {rumor_name} out {rumor_dir}. If there's treasure there, the Brotherhood would like first refusal.
Talk on the dock: {rumor_name}, out {rumor_dir}, {rumor_dist}. The dice say you should go. I loaded the dice, but still.
smuggler.rumor.none: No rumours worth the salt right now. The sea's gone quiet, and quiet's bad for business.
Nothing on the water lately but fish, Candles and weather. Ask me after the next run.
Word on the dock is there's no word. Rare, that.
If I knew of anything good nearby, I'd have pinched it already. So, no.
smuggler.seafolk: A merfolk trader once swapped me a handful of pearls for a jar of cinnamon. Best deal I ever made, and I think the merfolk thought the same.
Merfolk laugh at our sloop. I've seen them bob up by the hull, giggling. I don't know what's funny about it. Everything, apparently.
There's a rule in the Brotherhood: we don't cheat the merfolk. They know every rock and current, and an angry merfolk can sink you just by not mentioning a reef.
The Prismari, now, they're another matter. Tall, spined, one great eye, way down in the deep. Never seen one. Never want to. Well. Maybe once.
Old hands say the Prismari built the monuments, those sea-stone halls full of guardians. Same eye as on the Old Tide ruins. Funny, that.
A merfolk child once followed our sloop all night, curious, and kept quiet the whole run. Best lookout we ever had.
I hear the merfolk have whole towns of coral, lit up like a market at night. Imagine the trade. Imagine a tax collector trying to swim there.
If you ever see a single green light deep under your boat, it's polite to row away. A Prismari, some say. They don't like being stared at.
The merfolk know where all the wrecks are. Ask nicely and bring something sweet, and you might get a hint. Or a fish in the face. Depends on the merfolk.
smuggler.work: Crates up, crates down, crates in, crates out. Smuggling is mostly a lot of crates.
Every crate gets a mark only the Brotherhood can read: a knot, a notch, a smudge of tar. The Candles have been trying to read them for years.
Wet nights we row the cargo out to the buoys in the dark. Dry nights we stack it high in the rock. Every night we count it twice.
Pepper sneezes are the enemy. You learn to sneeze into your elbow, silently, in a boat, in the dark. It's a skill.
We patch the sloop's sails ourselves. Patches on patches. If the Candles ever see it in daylight, they'll laugh themselves into the sea.
Watching for sails is half the job. The lookout up top can spot a Tidewatch boat before it spots us. Usually.
Silk has to stay dry, spices have to stay sealed and pearls have to stay counted. Pearls walk off if you don't count them.
The lantern up top talks to boats at sea. Two shorts and a long: all clear. A long and a long: Candles. Short, long, short: bring the cat in.
Everything goes in the chief's ledger, every crate and every coin. No names, of course. Just marks.
Hiding cargo is an art: under fish, inside loaves, in a hollow plank. Once we hid cinnamon in a Tidewatch officer's hat. Long story.
The trick to unloading is speed and silence. The trick to loading is not dropping crates on your foot. I'm still working on that one.
We sell to inland traders, river barges, and a baker who doesn't ask questions. The baker gets the best cinnamon. Look after your bakers.
Every coin's split fair. Share the salt even, says the Article. Nobody here's ever been short-changed. Not even the cat.
Scraping barnacles off the sloop's hull. Not glamorous. Necessary. Barnacles slow you down, and slow gets you caught.
warden.adventure: Going out? Tell the fort which way first. If you don't come back, we'll know where to look.
The drowned are worse the deeper you go, and the ones dripping gold near the old wrecks are the worst of all.
If you find the Golden Heron, mind its captain. Ysolde Marrow went down with her ship, and sailors say she still keeps it.
Watch for Old Tide stonework under the water: sea-stone, dark stone and one great carved eye. The guardians there don't like visitors.
Buy a storm glass from a lighthouse keeper before you go. A sailor without one has a short career.
If you spot raiders, light anything you can and get back to a fort. That's not cowardice. That's the plan.
The Northward is out in the frozen north somewhere, locked in ice. Arvid Strand's crew is still aboard, the stories say. Not cheerful company, I'd guess.
Smugglers hide in hollow sea stacks. If you find one, tell the Tidewatch. Or don't, and tell me what their pepper smells like.
There's an old diving bell off the coast somewhere. Wexley's. Whatever went wrong on his last dive might still be down there.
The coast is long. A fort every so often, a light every so often, and between them, just you. Go carefully.
warden.chat: The Tide Log has every tide, every sail and every drowned we've seen since this fort was built. Some pages just say "fog."
We keep the light. That's the Tidewatch saying. A lighthouse, a brazier, a lantern on a pole: somebody keeps it lit.
Corwen, the First Keeper, kept a driftwood fire alive on a bare rock for three nights so a wrecked crew could find the shore. Every warden learns that before learning to hold a spear.
The drowned come up on dark nights, mostly near the reef. Every one goes in the Tide Log. The captain likes tallies.
The Brotherhood runs pepper and silk right under our noses. We catch about one boat in ten. The other nine wave.
There's a sloop we've chased for years. Every time we hail it and ask whose boat it is, a voice calls back "Maybe." Every Brotherhood boat is the Maybe, apparently.
The Briners call us "the Candles," because we keep lights. I can't decide if it's an insult. It sounds a bit like a compliment.
Every Tidewatch fort has a cat called Barnacle, after the ship's cat that floated ashore from the Golden Heron. Ours outranks me in the Tide Log.
Fort Hake wins the Lantern Shoot every year: archery by lantern light, every fort on the coast. I'm sure they cheat. I can't prove they cheat.
When I was sworn in, they tied a blue cord round my wrist. You wear it till it rots, then tie on another. Salt rots them fast.
The brazier on the keep is our loudest word. Lit means storm, or raiders, or come quick. It never means all's well. That's what quiet is for.
Raiders come in longboats, low and fast, on moonless nights. Our archers on the wall are the first to know and the last to sleep.
The sea gate's portcullis sticks every spring. Rust. We hang off the chains and swear at it until it moves.
The worst duty here is scraping barnacles off the boat. The second worst is the soup. Eating the soup counts as a duty.
Salt gets into armour, into hinges, into bowstrings. Into the soup, too, which is the only thing it improves.
We drill every morning: knights at the dummies, archers at the targets, everyone on the stairs until our knees file a complaint.
You can hear the whole sea from the wall at night. You learn its noises: wave, wave, seal, wave, drowned. That last one gets the bell.
Most lighthouse keepers stood these walls once. Now they get a whole tower to themselves and nobody shouting drill at dawn. Lucky.
When a storm comes in from the west, the whole fort hums. You feel it in your teeth.
A fisher once asked if we get bored out here. I pointed at the drowned crawling up the sea steps. Not bored. Damp.
The Tide Log is the only book here. The best bit is three pages a warden wrote about a gull that stole a boot.
Our boat's called the Steady. It isn't.
Barnacle caught a crab and brought it to the keep. It went in the Tide Log as "a capture."
