We patrol the reef by boat twice a day. Mostly we find driftwood and very surprised fish.
If a light goes dark anywhere on the coast, every fort lights its brazier. A chain of fires. Then somebody rows out to find out why.
Our archers can hit a bobbing bottle at sixty paces. In calm water. On a good day. Never in front of Fort Hake.
The knights carry shields painted blue with the white light. Some paint little waves round the rim. The captain pretends not to notice.
Being a warden means standing still in the rain for hours and being glad of it. Strange job. Good job.
The pay is poor, the food is worse, and the view is the best in the world.
Never trust a calm sea in the evening. It's only catching its breath.
Fog's the worst. In fog the drowned can walk right up the steps. So can smugglers. So can the cook, with the soup.
Captain {captain} writes the Tide Log in a hand so neat you could frame it. Even the entries about the soup.
warden.chat.close: I'd stand a watch for you, {player}. Any wall, any night. That's what a friend is, in the Tidewatch.
If anything ever happened to you out there, I'd row out myself. Don't tell the captain I said so; it breaks three different rules.
I've half a mind to ask the captain to make you an honorary warden. You'd need a blue cord. I have a spare.
Of everyone who's come through the sea gate, you're my favourite. Barnacle's second. Don't tell Barnacle.
I don't say this often, but it's good to have someone out here who isn't wearing a tabard.
When the night watch is long, I think about the people who come back. You always come back. Keep doing that.
Here. Tie this round your wrist. It's just a blue cord. It means you're one of us, as far as I'm concerned.
warden.chat.new: This is a Tidewatch fort. We guard the coast against the drowned, raiders and storms. Mostly storms; they never stop coming.
This is {place}: wall, keep, brazier, sea gate. If you hear the bell, get inside the keep and stay there.
I'm {name}. If you need anything, ask. If you need anything interesting, ask the captain.
Don't wander onto the wall at night without calling out first. Our archers are jumpy, and good.
If anything odd happens to you at sea, come and tell us. It all goes in the Tide Log.
Visitors can stay inside the wall. Just don't touch the brazier. Lighting it by accident would wake half the coast.
warden.greet: Halt! Oh, you're no raider. Welcome to {place}, then.
We keep the light. Welcome, friend of the coast.
Ahoy! Mind the weed on the sea steps; we've lost more wardens to those steps than to the drowned.
Warden {name}, of the Tidewatch. State your business, or just stand there and enjoy the spray.
A visitor! I'll have to write you in the Tide Log. Don't worry, you're in good company: three gulls and a crab.
Welcome to the fort, {player}. Keep your hands where I can see them. Joking. Mostly.
Light's lit, sea's calm, and here's a new face. Not a bad {time} at {place} after all.
Hello there. If you've come to join the Tidewatch, the captain's in the keep. If you've come for the soup, I'm sorry.
Ahoy, {player}. Sea gate's open, wall's manned, kettle's on. Come in.
Greetings from the Tidewatch. We're the ones who stand on walls in the rain so you don't have to.
Welcome to {place}. Wipe your boots; the captain inspects the floors.
You came in by boat? Brave. The current round the reef has eaten three of our boats this year. The wardens swam.
Hail and well met. Not a raider, not a drowned, not a Briner. Already a better visitor than most.
Oh, a guest! Everyone stand up straight; there's a guest.
Ahoy! You're dripping on my nice clean wall. That's all right. So is the sea.
Welcome. Barnacle the fort cat has inspected you from the battlements and found you acceptable.
Ho there. Don't mind the ballista; it only points at you out of habit.
warden.greet.evening: Evening. Brazier's stacked, watch is posted. We keep the light.
Good evening, {player}. The sun's going down, so the drowned will be coming up. Stay inside the wall.
Evening. Supper was fish pie. Don't ask what kind of fish; the cook doesn't know either.
Evening already? The days fly when you spend them scraping salt off your armour.
Evening, friend. Hear the gulls going quiet? That's the sea telling the night watch it's their turn.
warden.greet.friend: {player}! I told the others you'd be back. Nobody would bet against me, which was very wise of them.
Friend of the fort! Come up on the wall and stand a watch with me; it's dull without you.
There you are. Barnacle's been sitting by the sea gate as if waiting for somebody.
{player}, welcome back. Captain {captain} has you in the Tide Log as "Friend of the Tidewatch." That's not nothing.
Ah, our favourite landlubber. Or are you a sealubber by now? You've been out there long enough.
Back again! Pull up a crate. I saved you a ship's biscuit. Sorry, it's the hard kind. They're all the hard kind.
Good to see a friendly face. All the others here are friendly too, but I've seen them every day for a year.
warden.greet.morning: Morning, {player}. The dawn watch just changed. I've been staring at the sea since midnight and it's still there.
Good morning! Drill in the yard soon. Watch if you like; we fall over less in the mornings.
Morning. Quiet night: no drowned, no raiders, one very confused seal.
Morning tide's in. That's when we check the sea gate chains for weed.
Morning! Breakfast is hardtack and salt pork. So is lunch. So is supper.
warden.greet.night: Halt, who goes there? Oh, it's you, {player}. Can't be too careful at night.
Quietly, now. Night watch. Every splash out there gets a second look.
Out at night? Keep near the lanterns. The drowned like the dark water by the reef.
Late for a visit, {player}. It's cold on the wall, but the stars are good company.
Shh. Hear that? Just a wave. Probably just a wave. It goes in the Tide Log anyway: "probably a wave."
warden.greet.stranger: Don't know your face. That's no crime here, but I'll be watching you all the same. Welcome.
A stranger. Name and purpose, for the Tide Log. Or just a name. Or just wave, and I'll write "waved."
You're not from round here. Nobody's from round here; it's a rock in the sea. Come in.
New to the coast? Rule one: the drowned come up on dark nights. Rule two: never eat the soup.
I'm meant to search you for contraband. Pepper? Silk? No? Good. You're cleaner than the last three fishing boats.
Strangers get a warden's welcome: a nod, a squint and the second-best stool.
If you're Brotherhood, you're terrible at hiding it. If you're not, welcome to the fort.
warden.heart: Standing on a wall in the rain doesn't feel heroic. But every boat that gets home safe is because somebody did.
I miss home sometimes. Then I think: somebody's home is that light out there, and I help keep it lit.
The back of the Tide Log has names in it: wardens who didn't come home. We read them on the longest night of the year. It's quiet, after.
The people here are my family now. Loud, salty, badly fed family.
I'm not brave, you know. I'm scared every time the bell rings. I just go up the stairs anyway.
When the sun comes up after a bad night and you count heads and they're all there, it's the best feeling in the world.
Sometimes I envy the keepers. One light, one rock, all that quiet. Then I remember they cook for themselves.
We keep the light. I used to think it was about the brazier. It's about each other.
If I ever leave the Tidewatch, I'll still wake at the change of watch every night. You never really stop standing guard.
warden.held.axe: An axe! The brazier always needs firewood. You wouldn't be in a chopping mood?
Careful with that near the boat. The last warden who chopped near the boat sank it.
warden.held.boat: A boat! Heading out? Tell us which way, so the Tide Log knows where to look.
Keep your boat in the lee of the wall. The current round the reef eats boats.
warden.held.book: A book! Real reading. All we have here is the Tide Log, and I know how it ends: "fog."
Keeping your own log? Good. Every sailor should. Every warden must.
warden.held.bow: A bow! Our archers will want to see your draw. Don't be nervous. Be very nervous.
If you can hit a bobbing bottle at sixty paces, the Tidewatch wants you. Fort Hake especially wants you not to.
warden.held.bucket: A bucket! The boat's always leaking. Want a job?
Handy, that. We bail the boat every morning and the sea gate every storm.
warden.held.compass: A compass. Good. Too many sailors steer by guessing, and the sea doesn't reward guessing.
Watch the needle near the fort; the old iron in the walls makes it wander.
warden.held.diamond: A diamond! Hide it. The Brotherhood can smell those from a league away.
That's worth more than a whole fort's pay for a year. Probably more than the fort.
warden.held.emerald: Emeralds. Traders' money. Smugglers like them too. Not that I'm saying anything. I'm just looking at you.
Green as the reef at noon. Don't flash that about by the sea gate; it makes the knights nervous.
warden.held.fish: Fish! Don't give it to the cook. Cook it yourself; you'll do it better.
Barnacle will follow you all round the fort now. You've only yourself to blame.
warden.held.fishing_rod: Fishing off the wall is allowed when you're off watch. Officially.
A rod! Catch something better than the cook manages and I'll be your friend forever.
warden.held.flower: A flower! Nothing grows on a reef but weed and barnacles. Let me just look at it a moment.
For the fort? It can go in a helmet on the windowsill. That's the closest thing to a vase we have.
warden.held.food: Is that {item}? Real food? Don't let the knights see. Or our archers. Or me. Too late.
That smells better than anything our mess has ever served, and I can't even tell what it is.
warden.held.gold: Gold! Mind you're not taken for a Briner. Or for a drowned off the Golden Heron.
Drop a coin for Ysolde when you pass deep water, the old wardens say. For luck.
warden.held.map: A map! Show me. See, we're here, the reef's there, and Fort Hake's over there somewhere, being smug.
If that's one of the keepers' charts, trust the margins. The keepers write the good bits in the margins.
warden.held.ore: That {item} would make good fittings for the portcullis, if a smith ever came out this far.
Ore? The fort could always use more iron. Everything here rusts by Thursday.
warden.held.pearl: A pearl! The Brotherhood runs those past us all the time. You didn't get that from a smuggler, did you?
Pearls come from the warm shallows, from clams as big as barrels. Or out of Briners' pockets.
warden.held.pickaxe: Thinking of tunnelling? This fort sits on a reef. Down here, a tunnel is just a leak with ambitions.
Mining at sea is mostly a good way to flood things.
warden.held.potion: A potion? If it's for breathing under water, I'd like three.
Whatever's in that, keep it away from the soup. It might improve it, and the cook would be insulted.
warden.held.shell: A shell from the deep. The old wardens said a shell like that holds the sound of a storm.
That's from deep water. You've been diving where the drowned are. Brave.
warden.held.shield: A good shield. The knights here paint theirs blue with a white light. Yours would look smart that way.
Hold your shield high on the sea steps. The drowned throw tridents.
warden.held.shovel: A shovel. Not much digging on a fort built on a reef, but the wall always needs the gull mess shovelled off.
Treasure hunting? Everyone with a shovel is. The treasure's always under the sea.
warden.held.spyglass: A spyglass! Our archers would trade their best bowstrings for one of those.
Come up on the wall with that and tell me if that's a fishing boat or the Maybe. I can never tell.
warden.held.sword: Good blade. Keep it oiled; salt air eats a sword faster than any drowned.
That's a fair sword. The knights here will want to spar. Say no; they never stop.
warden.held.tnt: Put that down slowly. Slower. Good. Now please never bring it near the brazier.
Blasting powder? On a fort full of oil and lamps? Half the fort would fall over and the other half would fall in.
warden.held.torch: A light! We keep the light. You're practically one of us.
Careful with that near the brazier. That's a lot of oil to explain in the Tide Log.
warden.held.trident: A trident! You took that off a drowned. Well done; those tips are nasty.
That's a drowned's weapon. The armoury hangs one on the wall for every hundred drowned we send back. We have a lot of tridents.
warden.joke: Why did the warden take a ladder up to the wall? The captain said to step up the watch.
How can you tell a Fort Hake archer has won the Lantern Shoot? Don't worry. They'll tell you. For a year.
What do you call a smuggler without a boat? A swimmer. And a smuggler with a boat? Maybe.
A drowned walked up the sea steps once. "Name and purpose?" "Blub." So "Blub" went in the Tide Log. True story.
Why don't wardens play cards on the wall? The gulls keep taking tricks.
What's the difference between our soup and sea water? The sea water's been boiled less.
The Briners call us Candles. We call them Briners. Barnacle calls us both "the people with fish." Barnacle's the smartest of us.
Why did the knight take a fishing rod on patrol? To catch the drowned. It didn't work. It did catch lunch.
I asked for a day's leave. The captain looked at the sea and said, "Where would you go?" Fair point, really.
How many wardens does it take to light the brazier? Four. One to light it and three to write it in the Tide Log.
What did the fort say to the storm? Nothing. Forts don't talk. But if they did, it would be rude.
warden.news: Two drowned came up the sea steps last night. Both back in the sea now, and both in the Tide Log.
The boat's sprung a leak again. Somebody's bailing it this very minute, with a helmet. Not their own, I hope.
A fishing boat came in with "fish" that smelled of cinnamon. Brotherhood, sure as tides. They were gone while we were still sniffing.
Word is Fort Hake has practised for the Lantern Shoot all year. We've been practising too. In our heads.
The storm glass we bought from a keeper has gone cloudy. Rain coming. The cook's moved the soup indoors, for all the good it does.
Barnacle had kittens. Or Barnacle found kittens. Either way, there are more cats than there were. The Tide Log is unclear.
A merchant saw a dark sloop slip round the point without lights. The Maybe again, probably.
Our archers spotted longboats on the horizon at dusk. Probably fishers. We lit every lantern on the wall anyway.
The brazier chimney cracked in the cold. Somebody has to climb up and patch it. Somebody is going to be me.
A crate washed up against the wall this morning, full of silk. The captain says it's evidence. I say it's very nice silk.
Captain {captain} has doubled the night watch and won't say why. That usually means longboats.
warden.night: Night watch is the real work: eyes on the water, ears on the wind, and one hand on the bell rope.
See the lights out there? Fishing boats, a lighthouse, maybe a Brotherhood sloop with its lantern hooded. The sea's busier at night than people think.
The drowned come up when the moon's dark. Tonight's a dark one. Stay close to the lanterns.
I like the hour before dawn. Coldest, quietest, and you watch the whole sea turn grey like a page being written on.
Sometimes at night you hear singing out on the water. The captain says it's seals. I've never met a seal that could hold a tune.
Watch the lighthouse out there. While it's lit, all's well. If it goes dark, we light the brazier and somebody rows.
Night on the wall is when you think: about home, about the sea, about whether the soup's still on the fire. The soup is always on the fire.
warden.past: I swam the gate the night I was sworn. Every new warden does: out the sea gate, round the reef and back, in the dark. Coldest I've ever been.
In the Three-Day Blow the brazier burned three nights straight. We took turns feeding it in the rain. Every light on the coast held. Every one.
Fort Hake lost their boat in the Three-Day Blow. Found it a month later, up a tree inland. We still send them acorns.
I've been posted at more than one fort. The sea's different at each. The soup's the same.
There was a raid, years back. Longboats on a moonless night. Our archers saw the oars glint, and the bell rang before the first boat reached the reef.
I saw the Northward once, I swear it: a ship running north under full sail, late in the year. Everyone on the coast says that, though. Can't all be right.
The oldest Tide Log gives the Heron Gale four words: "Green sky. Great ship lost." Then three blank pages, as if nobody could bear to write more.
When I was a recruit, the old sergeant made us polish the brazier till we could see our faces in it. Then it rained. Then we did it again.
Old Wexley, the diving bell fellow, came through for a salvage permit. Later his barge was found riding at anchor over the bell, with nobody aboard.
My first drowned came up the sea steps on my first night. I dropped my spear; it dropped its trident. We stared at each other. Then I remembered I had a sword.
Before the Tidewatch I did a bit of everything, badly. Now I do one thing badly, in a tabard.
There was a winter the bay froze. We walked out to check the moorings, roped together like a string of sausages.
warden.player.damaged: That's barely holding together. Salt eats metal; mend it before your next fight.
Your gear's seen better days. We've no smith out here, just a hammer and good intentions.
warden.player.diamond: Diamond armour! Don't fall off the sea gate; you'd sink straight down to the drowned.
Look at that. Fort Hake would weep with envy, then polish theirs twice as hard.
warden.player.fire: You're on fire! The sea! Use the sea! It's everywhere!
Fire! Off the wall! No, wait, the sea steps! Either! Go!
warden.player.hungry: You look hungry. I'd offer you the soup, but I like you. Have a biscuit instead.
Hungry? There's salt pork in the mess. It's salty and it's pork. That's all I can promise.
warden.player.hurt: You're bleeding on the sea steps. Sit down. Our healing is mostly bandages and shouting, but it works.
Drowned got you? Sit by the brazier. I'll fetch bandages, and you can tell me which way it went.
warden.player.leather: Leather. Good for the sea. Floats, mostly. Smells of fish after a week.
Leather's sensible on the water. Rub tallow into it or the salt will crack it.
warden.player.unarmored: No armour? On a coast full of drowned? Brave, or new. Probably new.
You're not wearing a stitch of armour. The sea's no place for that, friend.
warden.rumor: The Tide Log has a note about {rumor_name}, out {rumor_dir}. Our patrols never went that far, but a fisher swore to it.
Fishers talk about {rumor_name}, {rumor_dir} of the fort. Call it {rumor_dist}. Worth a look, if you've the boat.
Hunting adventure? Try {rumor_dir}. Word is there's {rumor_name} that way, {rumor_dist}.
You can't see it from the keep, but there's {rumor_name} out {rumor_dir}, they say: {rumor_dist}, by the fishers' reckoning.
A merchant reported {rumor_name}, {rumor_dir} of here. It went in the Tide Log with a question mark.
Out {rumor_dir} there's {rumor_name}. I've always wanted to look. I've always been on watch.
Our archers see lights out {rumor_dir} some nights, and a fisher says there's {rumor_name} that way. Probably connected. Probably.
There's {rumor_name}, {rumor_dir} of {place}, {rumor_dist}. Take a friend, a lantern and a storm glass.
Ask any fisher about the {rumor_dir} and you'll hear about {rumor_name}. Then you'll hear about their aunt. Leave after the first part.
Sail {rumor_dir} and you'll find {rumor_name}, they say. Come back and tell us; the Tide Log likes an ending.
warden.rumor.none: Nothing in the Tide Log worth a sail lately. Drowned, fog, fish. The usual.
No word of anything out there. The fishers have gone quiet, which means either nothing's happening or everything is.
I've heard nothing new. Ask a lighthouse keeper; they hear more than any fort.
The sea's keeping its secrets this season. Ask again after the next storm; storms shake things loose.
warden.seafolk: Our archers swear they've seen merfolk out by the reef at dawn, tails flashing. They wave at the wall. We wave back. Officially.
Merfolk don't come near the fort much. Can't blame them. One whiff of our soup would scare anyone off.
A merfolk once surfaced by the sea gate and asked for whoever was in charge, very politely, to report drowned near their reef town. Into the Tide Log it went.
The Prismari, sailors call them: tall folk of the deep, spines down the back, one great eye. The old Tide Logs mention lights in deep water. Maybe it was them.
Some old hands say the Prismari built those sea-stone monuments in the deep, where the guardians swim. I'm not diving down to ask.
The merfolk know the sea better than any fort. When they say a storm's coming, we stack the brazier without arguing.
I once saw a carving of one great eye on an old sea-stone, and later heard a sailor describe a Prismari's face. Same eye. I didn't sleep well.
Merfolk children race our patrol boat sometimes. They always win. It's very bad for morale.
There's a rule in the Tidewatch: merfolk in trouble get the same help as anyone. The sea doesn't care who has legs.
warden.work: Every tide goes in the Tide Log: the time, the height, the wind, every sail and every drowned. It's dull, right up until the day it isn't.
Morning drill: knights to the dummies, archers to the targets. Then everyone scrapes salt off everything.
We patrol the reef by boat twice a day, looking for drowned, raiders, wrecks and whatever else the sea coughs up.
The brazier's kept stacked and dry. When it's needed, there's no time to go looking for kindling.
We search fishing boats that come too close. Usually it's fish. Once it was a crate of pepper under the fish. That was a good day.
Checking the gate chains, oiling the portcullis, tarring the boat. A fort is mostly maintenance and shouting.
Our archers count every sail on the horizon. The knights check every boat that comes in. The captain checks us.
Before a storm we bring the boat inside the sea gate and lash down everything that moves. Then we lash down the cook.
Drowned with tridents are the dangerous ones. You learn to watch the throwing arm.
We keep the light. That means the brazier, the lanterns and each other. And the Tide Log, which keeps us.
A warden's kit: a helmet, a blade or a bow, a dry cloak, a wet cloak, and a sense of humour about the second one.
When a lighthouse flashes red, we row. Doesn't matter the weather. Doesn't matter the hour.
The ballistae on the wall need restringing every month. Salt and damp rot the cords, like everything else here.
We watch the sky as much as the sea. A green sky before a storm means a bad one. The old Tide Log says the Heron Gale came in green.
Guard duty sounds dull, and it is, right up to the moment it very much isn't.
